Chapter 2: Linear Algebra for Macroeconomic Systems

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Input-Output Matrices, Eigenvalues, and Economic Structure

“The beauty of mathematics is that the same abstract structure — a system of linear equations — describes both the flow of goods between industries and the stability of a business cycle model.”

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 4 (circular flow, input-output analysis); Ch. 6 (data and econometric methods); Ch. 9 (IS–LM as a simultaneous system); Ch. 27 (RBC model, matrix solution) [P:Ch.4, P:Ch.6, P:Ch.9, P:Ch.27]

2.1 Why Linear Algebra? Economic Systems as Matrix Problems¶

A recurring structure in macroeconomics is the simultaneous equation system: a set of conditions that must hold jointly, involving multiple endogenous variables that are all determined together. The IS–LM model [P:Ch.9] is a 2×2 system determining (Y∗,i∗)(Y^*, i^*)(Y∗,i∗) from the intersection of two curves. The input-output model [P:Ch.4] is an n×nn \times nn×n system determining production levels across all sectors simultaneously. The log-linearized DSGE model of Part VII is a k×kk \times kk×k system of expectational difference equations. In each case, the right language is linear algebra.

Beyond solving systems, linear algebra provides the tools for:

  • Stability analysis: whether a dynamic system returns to equilibrium after a shock depends on the eigenvalues of its transition matrix — a central concept in Chapters 4, 14, and 28.

  • Dimensionality reduction: eigendecomposition reveals which directions in the state space matter most, which underlies the spectral analysis of time series and the solution algorithms for DSGE models.

  • Efficient computation: the matrix operations +.× (multiply) and ⌹ (divide/solve) in APL, and their analogues in NumPy and Julia’s LinearAlgebra, are the workhorses of every numerical algorithm in this book.

This chapter develops the linear algebra toolkit with these applications in mind. Every definition is illustrated with an economic example; every theorem is used somewhere in the book.

2.2 Vectors and Matrices as Economic Objects¶

2.2.1 Economic Vectors¶

A vector x∈Rn\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^nx∈Rn is an ordered list of nnn real numbers. In macroeconomics, vectors appear as:

  • State vectors in dynamic models: st=(kt,At)\mathbf{s}_t = (k_t, A_t)st​=(kt​,At​) in the RBC model, where ktk_tkt​ is the capital stock and AtA_tAt​ is the technology level.

  • Output vectors in input-output analysis: x=(x1,x2,…,xn)′\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)'x=(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)′ where xix_ixi​ is gross output of industry iii.

  • Impulse vectors in VAR models: ej\mathbf{e}_jej​ is the jjj-th standard basis vector, representing a unit shock to variable jjj.

Definition 2.1 (Inner Product). The inner product of two vectors u,v∈Rn\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^nu,v∈Rn is:

⟨u,v⟩=u′v=∑i=1nuivi.\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \mathbf{u}'\mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i.⟨u,v⟩=u′v=i=1∑n​ui​vi​.
(1)

The inner product p′q\mathbf{p}'\mathbf{q}p′q where p\mathbf{p}p is a price vector and q\mathbf{q}q is a quantity vector gives the value of the basket at those prices — the fundamental operation underlying both GDP measurement and the computation of price indices [P:Ch.3.1].

2.2.2 Matrices as Linear Transformations¶

A matrix A∈Rm×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}A∈Rm×n represents a linear map T:Rn→RmT: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^mT:Rn→Rm via T(x)=AxT(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}T(x)=Ax. The action of AAA on a vector transforms it — rotating, scaling, projecting — without any nonlinear distortion. This linearity is exactly why linearized DSGE models are tractable: every period’s state vector is a linear function of the previous state and the current shocks.

Definition 2.2 (Matrix Multiplication). For A∈Rm×kA \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times k}A∈Rm×k and B∈Rk×nB \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}B∈Rk×n, the product C=AB∈Rm×nC = AB \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}C=AB∈Rm×n has elements:

cij=∑l=1kailblj=ai′bj,c_{ij} = \sum_{l=1}^k a_{il} b_{lj} = \mathbf{a}_i' \mathbf{b}_j,cij​=l=1∑k​ail​blj​=ai′​bj​,
(2)

where ai′\mathbf{a}_i'ai′​ is the iii-th row of AAA and bj\mathbf{b}_jbj​ is the jjj-th column of BBB. Matrix multiplication is associative (AB)C=A(BC)(AB)C = A(BC)(AB)C=A(BC) and distributive A(B+C)=AB+ACA(B+C) = AB + ACA(B+C)=AB+AC, but not commutative in general: AB≠BAAB \neq BAAB=BA.

In APL, matrix multiplication is the inner product A +.× B — read as “sum of products of corresponding elements, by column.” This primitive is the single most-used operation in the entire book.

2.3 Matrix Inversion and the Solution of Linear Systems¶

2.3.1 The Inverse Matrix¶

Definition 2.3 (Matrix Inverse). A square matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is invertible (or nonsingular) if there exists a matrix A−1A^{-1}A−1 such that A−1A=AA−1=InA^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I_nA−1A=AA−1=In​, where InI_nIn​ is the n×nn \times nn×n identity matrix. AAA is invertible if and only if det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0det(A)=0, equivalently, if and only if AAA has full rank nnn.

The system Ax=bA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b has a unique solution x∗=A−1b\mathbf{x}^* = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}x∗=A−1b when AAA is invertible.

In APL, A−1bA^{-1}\mathbf{b}A−1b is written b ⌹ A. The monadic form ⌹A computes A−1A^{-1}A−1 directly. The ⌹ primitive (called “domino” or “matrix divide”) calls LAPACK’s LU solver internally, so it is both convenient and numerically stable.

b ← 8 5                  ⍝ right-hand side (as a vector)
x ← b ⌹ A               ⍝ solution: x = A⁻¹b
x                        ⍝ should give 19 ¯30 (check: 2×19 + 1×(¯30) = 8 ✓)

⍝ Explicit inverse (use with care — solve directly when possible)

Ainv +.× b               ⍝ same result via explicit inverse

Note on numerical practice: Computing A−1A^{-1}A−1 explicitly and then multiplying is less numerically stable than solving Ax=bA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b directly. Always prefer b ⌹ A over (⌹A) +.× b in production code.

2.3.2 Cramer’s Rule¶

For small systems (2×2, 3×3), Cramer’s rule gives explicit closed-form solutions that are useful for comparative statics.

Theorem 2.1 (Cramer’s Rule). For the system Ax=bA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}Ax=b with A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n invertible, the iii-th component of the solution is:

xi∗=det⁡(Ai)det⁡(A),x_i^* = \frac{\det(A_i)}{\det(A)},xi∗​=det(A)det(Ai​)​,
(3)

where AiA_iAi​ is the matrix obtained by replacing the iii-th column of AAA with b\mathbf{b}b.

Proof sketch for 2×2. With A=(abcd)A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}A=(ac​bd​), b=(ef)\mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} e \\ f \end{pmatrix}b=(ef​):

det⁡(A)=ad−bc,det⁡(A1)=∣ebfd∣=ed−bf,det⁡(A2)=∣aecf∣=af−ce.\det(A) = ad - bc, \quad \det(A_1) = \begin{vmatrix} e & b \\ f & d \end{vmatrix} = ed - bf, \quad \det(A_2) = \begin{vmatrix} a & e \\ c & f \end{vmatrix} = af - ce.det(A)=ad−bc,det(A1​)=∣∣​ef​bd​∣∣​=ed−bf,det(A2​)=∣∣​ac​ef​∣∣​=af−ce.
(4)

Direct calculation: x1∗=(ed−bf)/(ad−bc)x_1^* = (ed - bf)/(ad - bc)x1∗​=(ed−bf)/(ad−bc), x2∗=(af−ce)/(ad−bc)x_2^* = (af - ce)/(ad - bc)x2∗​=(af−ce)/(ad−bc), which one can verify satisfies Ax∗=bA\mathbf{x}^* = \mathbf{b}Ax∗=b. □\square□

2.4 The Leontief Input-Output Model¶

The input-output model of Wassily Leontief (1941) is both an important economic framework and an elegant illustration of linear algebra in macroeconomics. It is the foundation of the production-side national accounts [P:Ch.4.5].

Definition 2.4 (Technical Coefficient Matrix). For an economy with nnn industries, the technical coefficient matrix A=[aij]A = [a_{ij}]A=[aij​] has element aija_{ij}aij​ equal to the dollar value of input from industry iii required to produce one dollar of gross output in industry jjj. Each column jjj represents the production recipe of industry jjj.

The accounting identity for gross output: each industry’s output equals its deliveries to other industries plus its deliveries to final demand d\mathbf{d}d:

x=Ax+d  ⟹  (I−A)x=d  ⟹  x=(I−A)−1d.\mathbf{x} = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{d} \implies (I - A)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d} \implies \mathbf{x} = (I-A)^{-1}\mathbf{d}.x=Ax+d⟹(I−A)x=d⟹x=(I−A)−1d.
(5)

Definition 2.5 (Leontief Inverse). The matrix L=(I−A)−1L = (I - A)^{-1}L=(I−A)−1 is the Leontief inverse or total requirements matrix. Its (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) element gives the total output of industry iii — direct plus all indirect upstream requirements — needed to deliver one dollar of final demand for industry jjj’s product.

Theorem 2.2 (Existence of the Leontief Inverse). (I−A)−1(I - A)^{-1}(I−A)−1 exists and has all non-negative elements if and only if all eigenvalues of AAA have modulus strictly less than 1. When this holds:

(I−A)−1=I+A+A2+A3+⋯=∑k=0∞Ak.(I-A)^{-1} = I + A + A^2 + A^3 + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^\infty A^k.(I−A)−1=I+A+A2+A3+⋯=k=0∑∞​Ak.
(6)

Proof of the series representation. For any matrix BBB with all eigenvalues inside the unit circle, Bk→0B^k \to \mathbf{0}Bk→0 as k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞. The partial sums SN=∑k=0NAkS_N = \sum_{k=0}^N A^kSN​=∑k=0N​Ak satisfy (I−A)SN=I−AN+1→I(I-A)S_N = I - A^{N+1} \to I(I−A)SN​=I−AN+1→I as N→∞N \to \inftyN→∞. The limit is therefore (I−A)−1(I-A)^{-1}(I−A)−1. □\square□

The economic interpretation of the series is the multiplier chain: the first term III represents direct demand; AdA\mathbf{d}Ad captures first-round intermediate input requirements; A2dA^2\mathbf{d}A2d captures second-round requirements; and so on. This is precisely the input-output analogue of the Keynesian spending multiplier [P:Ch.8].

The APL expression =⍨⍳n deserves explanation: ⍳n generates the vector 0 1 2 ... n-1 (with ⎕IO←0); =⍨ applies the outer product of equality to this vector with itself, yielding an n×nn \times nn×n identity matrix. This is a characteristic APL idiom — generating structured matrices from primitive operations.

2.5 Determinants, Rank, and Singularity¶

2.5.1 The Determinant¶

Definition 2.6 (Determinant). The determinant det⁡(A)\det(A)det(A) of a square matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is a scalar that measures the signed volume scaling factor of the linear transformation represented by AAA. For n=2n = 2n=2:

det⁡(abcd)=ad−bc.\det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc.det(ac​bd​)=ad−bc.
(7)

The determinant has several key properties:

  • det⁡(AB)=det⁡(A)det⁡(B)\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)det(AB)=det(A)det(B).

  • det⁡(A−1)=1/det⁡(A)\det(A^{-1}) = 1/\det(A)det(A−1)=1/det(A) when AAA is invertible.

  • det⁡(A′)=det⁡(A)\det(A') = \det(A)det(A′)=det(A).

  • AAA is invertible iff det⁡(A)≠0\det(A) \neq 0det(A)=0.

In macroeconomics, det⁡(A)\det(A)det(A) appears in Cramer’s rule (Section 2.3.2) and in the IS–LM multiplier formulas of Chapter 6. The sign of det⁡(I−A)\det(I - A)det(I−A) in the Leontief model determines whether the economy is productive.

2.5.2 Rank and Linear Independence¶

Definition 2.7 (Rank). The rank of a matrix AAA, denoted rank(A)\text{rank}(A)rank(A), is the dimension of the column space of AAA — the number of linearly independent columns. Equivalently, it is the number of nonzero singular values of AAA.

For the DSGE model identification problem (Chapter 41), rank conditions are central: a model is identified only if the Jacobian matrix mapping structural parameters to model predictions has full column rank.

2.6 Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors¶

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are the most important concepts in linear algebra for dynamic macroeconomics. The stability of any linear dynamic system — whether it converges to a steady state, oscillates, or explodes — is determined entirely by the eigenvalues of its transition matrix.

Definition 2.8 (Eigenvalue and Eigenvector). Let A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n. A scalar λ∈C\lambda \in \mathbb{C}λ∈C is an eigenvalue of AAA with corresponding eigenvector v≠0\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}v=0 if:

Av=λv.A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}.Av=λv.
(8)

The set of all eigenvalues is the spectrum of AAA, denoted σ(A)\sigma(A)σ(A). The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial:

p(λ)=det⁡(λI−A)=0.p(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A) = 0.p(λ)=det(λI−A)=0.
(9)

For n=2n = 2n=2, this gives the quadratic λ2−tr(A)λ+det⁡(A)=0\lambda^2 - \text{tr}(A)\lambda + \det(A) = 0λ2−tr(A)λ+det(A)=0, with roots:

λ1,2=tr(A)±tr(A)2−4det⁡(A)2.\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\text{tr}(A) \pm \sqrt{\text{tr}(A)^2 - 4\det(A)}}{2}.λ1,2​=2tr(A)±tr(A)2−4det(A)​​.
(10)

Note two useful identities: λ1+λ2=tr(A)\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \text{tr}(A)λ1​+λ2​=tr(A) and λ1λ2=det⁡(A)\lambda_1 \lambda_2 = \det(A)λ1​λ2​=det(A).

2.6.1 Eigenvalues and Stability¶

Theorem 2.3 (Stability of Linear Discrete-Time Systems). The system xt+1=Axt\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_txt+1​=Axt​ converges to 0\mathbf{0}0 from any initial condition if and only if all eigenvalues of AAA satisfy ∣λi∣<1|\lambda_i| < 1∣λi​∣<1. The system diverges if any ∣λi∣>1|\lambda_i| > 1∣λi​∣>1.

Theorem 2.4 (Stability of Linear Continuous-Time Systems). The system x˙=Ax\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}x˙=Ax converges to 0\mathbf{0}0 from any initial condition if and only if all eigenvalues of AAA satisfy Re(λi)<0\text{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0Re(λi​)<0.

These two theorems underlie all stability analysis in macroeconomics:

  • The Solow model’s convergence to the steady state (Chapter 10) corresponds to the continuous-time condition Re(λ)<0\text{Re}(\lambda) < 0Re(λ)<0 for the linearized ODE.

  • The Blanchard–Kahn condition for a unique stable solution to a DSGE model (Chapter 28) requires counting eigenvalues inside vs. outside the unit circle.

  • The determinacy condition ϕπ>1\phi_\pi > 1ϕπ​>1 for the Taylor rule (Chapter 28, [P:Ch.23.1]) translates into a requirement on the eigenvalues of the NK system’s transition matrix.

If AAA has nnn linearly independent eigenvectors v1,…,vn\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_nv1​,…,vn​ with eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​, form the matrix P=[v1∣⋯∣vn]P = [\mathbf{v}_1 | \cdots | \mathbf{v}_n]P=[v1​∣⋯∣vn​]. Then:

A=PDP−1,D=diag(λ1,…,λn).A = PDP^{-1}, \quad D = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n).A=PDP−1,D=diag(λ1​,…,λn​).
(11)

Powers are trivial: Ak=PDkP−1A^k = PD^kP^{-1}Ak=PDkP−1 where Dk=diag(λ1k,…,λnk)D^k = \text{diag}(\lambda_1^k, \ldots, \lambda_n^k)Dk=diag(λ1k​,…,λnk​).

2.7 The Spectral Decomposition and Symmetric Matrices¶

Many matrices in macroeconomics are symmetric: covariance matrices, Hessians, and the matrices arising from certain DSGE structures. Symmetric matrices have a particularly clean spectral structure.

Theorem 2.5 (Spectral Decomposition of Symmetric Matrices). If A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is symmetric, then:

  1. All eigenvalues are real.

  2. Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

  3. AAA has an orthogonal eigendecomposition A=QΛQ′A = Q\Lambda Q'A=QΛQ′ where QQQ is orthogonal (Q′Q=IQ'Q = IQ′Q=I) and Λ=diag(λ1,…,λn)\Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)Λ=diag(λ1​,…,λn​).

Definition 2.9 (Quadratic Form). For a symmetric matrix AAA and vector x\mathbf{x}x, the expression x′Ax\mathbf{x}'A\mathbf{x}x′Ax is a quadratic form. The sign of this form for all nonzero x\mathbf{x}x is determined entirely by the signs of the eigenvalues of AAA — which is why positive/negative definiteness of the Hessian determines whether a critical point is a minimum/maximum (Theorem 1.4).

In APL, the quadratic form x′Ax\mathbf{x}'A\mathbf{x}x′Ax:

Chapter 6 of this book develops this analysis fully, adding Cramer’s rule derivations for all policy multipliers and extending to the open economy (Mundell–Fleming).

2.9 The Jordan Normal Form and Defective Matrices¶

Not every matrix is diagonalisable. When a matrix has repeated eigenvalues and insufficient eigenvectors, we need the Jordan normal form.

Definition 2.10 (Jordan Block). A Jordan block of size mmm with eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ is the m×mm \times mm×m matrix:

Jm(λ)=(λ10⋯00λ1⋯0⋮⋱⋱⋮0⋯0λ10⋯00λ).J_m(\lambda) = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & \lambda & 1 \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \lambda \end{pmatrix}.Jm​(λ)=⎝⎛​λ0⋮00​1λ⋯⋯​01⋱00​⋯⋯⋱λ0​00⋮1λ​⎠⎞​.
(17)

Theorem 2.6 (Jordan Normal Form). Every square matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n (over C\mathbb{C}C) is similar to a block-diagonal matrix J=diag(Jm1(λ1),…,Jmr(λr))J = \text{diag}(J_{m_1}(\lambda_1), \ldots, J_{m_r}(\lambda_r))J=diag(Jm1​​(λ1​),…,Jmr​​(λr​)), where ∑mi=n\sum m_i = n∑mi​=n.

For the stability analysis of dynamic systems, Jordan blocks with eigenvalue ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1 still converge to zero, but more slowly than the diagonal case — the presence of the superdiagonal 1s means the kkk-th power of Jm(λ)J_m(\lambda)Jm​(λ) contains terms like (kj)λk−j\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}(jk​)λk−j, which still go to zero as k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞ when ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1.

In practice, most matrices arising in macroeconomic models are either diagonalisable or can be handled with the generalized Schur (QZ) decomposition (Chapter 28), so the Jordan form is primarily of theoretical importance.

2.10 Worked Example: Three-Sector Leontief Economy¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 4.5 (input-output analysis) [P:Ch.4.5]

Consider a three-sector economy (manufacturing, services, agriculture) with the following technical coefficient matrix:

A=(0.200.150.050.250.100.200.050.080.15),A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.20 & 0.15 & 0.05 \\ 0.25 & 0.10 & 0.20 \\ 0.05 & 0.08 & 0.15 \end{pmatrix},A=⎝⎛​0.200.250.05​0.150.100.08​0.050.200.15​⎠⎞​,
(18)

and final demand vector d=(120,80,50)′\mathbf{d} = (120, 80, 50)'d=(120,80,50)′.

Step 1: Verify AAA is productive. Compute ρ(A)=max⁡i∣λi∣\rho(A) = \max_i|\lambda_i|ρ(A)=maxi​∣λi​∣, the spectral radius of AAA. If ρ(A)<1\rho(A) < 1ρ(A)<1, the Leontief inverse exists.

The eigenvalues of AAA can be found from its characteristic polynomial. For a rough check, note that the maximum column sum of AAA is max⁡j∑iaij=0.50+0.33+0.40=0.50<1\max_j \sum_i a_{ij} = 0.50 + 0.33 + 0.40 = 0.50 < 1maxj​∑i​aij​=0.50+0.33+0.40=0.50<1. Since this column-sum norm bounds the spectral radius, ρ(A)≤0.50<1\rho(A) \leq 0.50 < 1ρ(A)≤0.50<1, confirming productivity.

Step 2: Compute the Leontief inverse L=(I−A)−1L = (I-A)^{-1}L=(I−A)−1.

I−A=(0.80−0.15−0.05−0.250.90−0.20−0.05−0.080.85).I - A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.80 & -0.15 & -0.05 \\ -0.25 & 0.90 & -0.20 \\ -0.05 & -0.08 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix}.I−A=⎝⎛​0.80−0.25−0.05​−0.150.90−0.08​−0.05−0.200.85​⎠⎞​.
(19)

Computing (I−A)−1(I-A)^{-1}(I−A)−1 numerically (shown below):

L≈(1.3270.2470.1230.4041.2140.3280.0940.1221.222).L \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1.327 & 0.247 & 0.123 \\ 0.404 & 1.214 & 0.328 \\ 0.094 & 0.122 & 1.222 \end{pmatrix}.L≈⎝⎛​1.3270.4040.094​0.2471.2140.122​0.1230.3281.222​⎠⎞​.
(20)

Step 3: Compute gross output x=Ld\mathbf{x} = L\mathbf{d}x=Ld.

x=Ld≈(1.3270.2470.1230.4041.2140.3280.0940.1221.222)(1208050)≈(185.8130.084.3).\mathbf{x} = L\mathbf{d} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1.327 & 0.247 & 0.123 \\ 0.404 & 1.214 & 0.328 \\ 0.094 & 0.122 & 1.222 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 120 \\ 80 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 185.8 \\ 130.0 \\ 84.3 \end{pmatrix}.x=Ld≈⎝⎛​1.3270.4040.094​0.2471.2140.122​0.1230.3281.222​⎠⎞​⎝⎛​1208050​⎠⎞​≈⎝⎛​185.8130.084.3​⎠⎞​.
(21)

Step 4: Interpretation. To deliver $120 of manufacturing to final demand, the economy must produce $185.8 of manufacturing gross output in total — the additional $65.8 supplies intermediate inputs to all three sectors through the full chain of upstream requirements.

Step 5: Multiplier. The total output multiplier for manufacturing final demand is ∑iLi1=1.327+0.404+0.094=1.825\sum_i L_{i1} = 1.327 + 0.404 + 0.094 = 1.825∑i​Li1​=1.327+0.404+0.094=1.825: one dollar of final demand for manufacturing generates $1.825 of total gross output across all sectors.

Exercise 2.2 (Python)¶

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.20, 0.15, 0.05],
              [0.25, 0.10, 0.20],
              [0.05, 0.08, 0.15]])
d = np.array([120, 80, 50])

n = A.shape[0]
L = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(n) - A)   # Leontief inverse
x = L @ d                            # gross output
print("Gross output:", x.round(2))
print("Output multipliers:", L.sum(axis=0).round(4))
print("Spectral radius:", max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(A))).round(4))

Exercise 2.3 (Julia)¶

using LinearAlgebra
A = [0.20 0.15 0.05;
     0.25 0.10 0.20;
     0.05 0.08 0.15]
d = [120.0, 80.0, 50.0]
L = inv(I - A)
x = L * d
println("Gross output: ", round.(x, digits=2))
println("Multipliers: ", round.(sum(L, dims=1), digits=4))
println("Spectral radius: ", maximum(abs.(eigvals(A))) |> x -> round(x, digits=4))

Exercise 2.4 (R)¶

A <- matrix(c(0.20,0.25,0.05, 0.15,0.10,0.08, 0.05,0.20,0.15), 3, 3)
d <- c(120, 80, 50)
n <- nrow(A)
L <- solve(diag(n) - A)
x <- L %*% d
cat("Gross output:", round(x, 2), "\n")
cat("Multipliers:", round(colSums(L), 4), "\n")
cat("Spectral radius:", round(max(abs(eigen(A)$values)), 4), "\n")

Exercise 2.7 — Perron–Frobenius (⋆⋆\star\star⋆⋆)¶

The Perron–Frobenius theorem states that a non-negative irreducible matrix AAA has a unique largest real eigenvalue λPF>0\lambda_{PF} > 0λPF​>0 (the Perron root) with a corresponding non-negative eigenvector. In the Leontief context, if λPF<1\lambda_{PF} < 1λPF​<1, the economy is productive. (a) Verify the Perron root numerically for the 3-sector matrix AAA above. (b) Find by bisection the largest value of a scalar multiplier α\alphaα such that αA\alpha AαA remains productive (i.e., λPF(αA)<1\lambda_{PF}(\alpha A) < 1λPF​(αA)<1). (c) Interpret economically.

2.12 Chapter Summary¶

This chapter developed the linear algebra toolkit for macroeconomic modeling.

Key results:

  • The Leontief inverse (I−A)−1=∑k=0∞Ak(I-A)^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty A^k(I−A)−1=∑k=0∞​Ak exists when the spectral radius ρ(A)<1\rho(A) < 1ρ(A)<1 and gives total (direct plus indirect) output requirements per unit of final demand.

  • Cramer’s rule provides explicit closed-form solutions for small linear systems — the foundation for IS–LM multiplier derivations in Chapter 6.

  • Eigenvalues determine stability: a discrete system xt+1=Axt\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_txt+1​=Axt​ is stable iff all ∣λi∣<1|\lambda_i| < 1∣λi​∣<1; a continuous system x˙=Ax\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}x˙=Ax is stable iff all Re(λi)<0\text{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0Re(λi​)<0.

  • Diagonalization A=PDP−1A = PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1 makes powers Ak=PDkP−1A^k = PD^kP^{-1}Ak=PDkP−1 trivial, enabling analytical and numerical computation of impulse response functions.

  • In APL: ⌹ solves linear systems and computes matrix inverses; +.× is matrix multiplication; =⍨⍳n generates the identity matrix; +⌿ computes column sums (output multipliers).

Connections forward: Chapter 3 uses eigenvalue analysis to classify the equilibria of differential equation systems. Chapter 4 applies it to difference equations and previews the Blanchard–Kahn condition. Chapter 6 uses Cramer’s rule to derive all IS–LM multipliers. Chapter 28 uses the generalized Schur (QZ) decomposition — an extension of eigendecomposition — to solve linear DSGE models.
